konular: Why Transformers: attention instead of recurrence
Input vectors and positional encoding (absolute, relative, RoPE)
Add & Norm: residual connection and LayerNorm
Distinct roles of attention and FFN, and the block stack
Model families: BERT, GPT, T5 and MLM

sorular.konu: Why Transformers: attention instead of recurrence
sorular.soru: What is the main reason the Transformer prefers attention over RNN/LSTM-style step-by-step processing?
secenekler: Attention reduces the number of parameters, making training cheaper
Attention processes all positions in parallel and creates direct paths between tokens
Attention carries order information implicitly in the dot product, so no extra signal is needed
Attention reduces memory by compressing a long sequence into a single fixed-size summary vector
sorular.aciklama: RNNs carry information step by step and parallelism is limited, whereas attention processes all positions in parallel and builds direct token-to-token paths. The claim that order information is implicit in the dot product is wrong; in fact position information must be supplied separately.

sorular.konu: Input vectors and positional encoding (absolute, relative, RoPE)
sorular.soru: Without positional encoding, why can self-attention not distinguish the sequences 'dog bites man' and 'man bites dog'?
secenekler: Because softmax weights sum to 1, order information is normalized away and lost
Because the embedding table gives the same word a different vector at each position, causing total confusion
Because the residual connection cannot pass the position vector to the next block, so order is erased
Because dot-product comparison is insensitive to order; the two sequences look like the same set of tokens
sorular.aciklama: Self-attention only compares content vectors, and the dot product contains no token order, so the same tokens in a different order look like the same set. The embedding table is position-independent: the same word gets the same token embedding, and any difference comes only from the added position vector.

sorular.konu: Input vectors and positional encoding (absolute, relative, RoPE)
sorular.soru: Which limitation of pure absolute positional encoding (sinusoidal or learned) motivates relative methods?
secenekler: The distance between tokens is not explicit; the model must learn it indirectly from pᵢ and pⱼ
The same word receives the same total input vector at every position, so order information is completely lost
The position signal is added only to Q and K and not to V, so the content is corrupted
The sinusoidal pattern is deterministic, so it is never updated during training
sorular.aciklama: Absolute methods answer the question 'which slot am I in?'; the distance between two tokens is not represented explicitly, and the model must infer it from pᵢ and pⱼ. That the sinusoidal pattern is fixed is true, but it is a difference from learned PE, not a limitation.

sorular.konu: Input vectors and positional encoding (absolute, relative, RoPE)
sorular.soru: In modern practice, how does RoPE use position information differently from the classical approach?
secenekler: By adding a learned position vector (learned PE) to the input embedding
By adding a deterministic sinusoidal position vector to the token embedding
By rotating Q and K according to their absolute positions, which gives attention a relative effect
By adding token-to-token offset information to the value vectors, which changes the weighted sum
sorular.aciklama: Instead of adding position to the input, RoPE rotates Q and K inside attention according to absolute position, and the effect behaves like relative position. Adding a position vector to the input embedding is the classical (learned/sinusoidal) absolute approach; RoPE differs precisely by not doing this.

sorular.soru: For the query q_it = [0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5] and the key k_tired = [1.0, 0.0, 0.5, 0.5] with dk = 4, what are the raw dot-product score and the score scaled by √dk for 'tired', respectively?
sorular.aciklama: The dot product is 0.5·1 + 0.5·0 + 0.5·0.5 + 0.5·0.5 = 1.0; dividing by √dk = √4 = 2 gives 0.50. The option '1.0 and 0.25' reflects the error of dividing by dk = 4 instead of √dk, and '2.0 and 1.00' is the score of the token 'animal'.

sorular.soru: Given the attention weights ('animal' 0.481, 'street' 0.227, 'tired' 0.292) and the value vectors (v_animal = [1,0,0,1], v_street = [0,1,0,1], v_tired = [1,1,1,0]), approximately what is the second component of the output vector for 'it'?
sorular.aciklama: Only v_street and v_tired have the value 1 in the second component: 0.227 + 0.292 = 0.519. 0.773 is the first component (animal + tired) and 0.708 is the fourth component (animal + street); one must note which value vector carries a 1 in which component.

sorular.soru: In multi-head attention, which mechanism lets the heads produce 'complementary views' of the same sequence?
secenekler: Each head takes a different part of the sequence (a local window) and processes only that part
The heads run sequentially; each head takes the previous head's output as input and updates it
The heads share the same WQ, WK, WV weights; only the softmax scaling factor differs between heads
Each head applies its own WQ, WK, WV to the same X; outputs are concatenated and mixed by WO
sorular.aciklama: Each head computes head_i = Attention(XW_i^Q, XW_i^K, XW_i^V); all heads see the same X but learn different projections, so they form different routing patterns, and the results are combined with Concat(...)W^O. The idea that heads process different parts of the sequence is wrong; the difference lies in the learned projections, not in the input.

sorular.soru: A model has sequence length n = 8192, dmodel = 4096, h = 32 heads and dhead = 128. What are the dimensions of a single head's Q_hK_hᵀ score matrix and of the concatenated output of all heads (the matrix fed into W_O), respectively?
sorular.aciklama: Multiplying Q_h (8192×128) by K_hᵀ (128×8192) gives an 8192×8192 score matrix, an n×n matrix independent of dhead; each of the 32 heads produces an 8192×128 output, and the concatenation is 8192×(32·128) = 8192×4096. The option '8192 × 8192 and 8192 × 128' confuses a single head's output with the concatenated result.

sorular.konu: Add & Norm: residual connection and LayerNorm
sorular.soru: What does LayerNorm in a Transformer normalize, and along which axis?
secenekler: One token vector across its own feature dimensions; independent of the batch
Each feature across all tokens in the sequence; it depends on the sequence length
Each feature across the examples in the mini-batch; it depends on batch statistics
The attention scores along each row; it makes the weights sum to 1 for every query
sorular.aciklama: LayerNorm computes μ and σ² over the d components of a single token vector; each token is normalized independently and no batch statistics are used. Normalizing over the mini-batch is the behavior of BatchNorm, and making each row sum to 1 is the job of softmax.

sorular.konu: Add & Norm: residual connection and LayerNorm
sorular.soru: If the residual (skip) connection in the Add & Norm step were removed, what would be lost?
secenekler: The guarantee that softmax attention weights are always positive and sum to exactly 1
Preservation of the old state; the sublayer would have to produce all of h′, not just Δh
The FFN's property of processing each position independently of other tokens' representations
LayerNorm's ability to restore a useful scale and shift through its γ and β parameters
sorular.aciklama: The sublayer only proposes an update (Δh), and the residual path carries the old h into the sum so that information is not lost; without the connection, each block would have to rewrite the vector from scratch. The softmax sum and the FFN's position independence are properties unrelated to the residual connection.

sorular.konu: Distinct roles of attention and FFN, and the block stack
sorular.soru: Which statement comparing the attention and FFN sublayers of a Transformer block is correct?
secenekler: Attention transforms each token independently; the FFN carries information across tokens
Both carry information across tokens; the only difference between them is that the FFN is nonlinear
Attention carries information across tokens; the FFN applies the same network to each position
The FFN learns different weights for each position; attention shares weights across all positions
sorular.aciklama: Attention is the 'tokens talk' step, where information comes from other positions; the FFN does not select other tokens and applies the same nonlinear transformation position by position. The first option reverses the roles, a common confusion; the FFN does not learn position-specific weights, and the 'same FFN' is shared across all positions.

sorular.soru: In a causal mask example, if the scaled scores are [1, 2, 1, 2] and the mask is [0, 0, −∞, −∞], which of the following is approximately the attention weights after softmax?
sorular.aciklama: The mask is added before softmax: [1, 2, −∞, −∞] → since exp(−∞) = 0, the last two positions get 0, and the first two become e¹/(e¹+e²) ≈ 0.27 and e²/(e¹+e²) ≈ 0.73. [0.13, 0.37, 0.13, 0.37] is the softmax of all four scores as if no mask were applied; [0.50, 0.50, 0, 0] is the error of giving the allowed positions equal weight regardless of the scores.

sorular.soru: While training a decoder-only model, the shifted-right target positions are computed in parallel; what happens if the causal mask is accidentally not applied?
secenekler: Training can no longer be parallelized; tokens must be generated one by one as in inference
Each position sees the next token it is supposed to predict directly through attention; the model 'cheats'
Cross-attention can no longer access the encoder output; the source sentence information is completely lost
Softmax weights can become negative; training becomes numerically unstable
sorular.aciklama: In training, all target positions are computed in parallel, so ensuring that position t does not see positions > t is achieved only by the causal mask; without it, the model reads the next token directly and next-token prediction becomes meaningless. The claim that parallelism would break is backwards: the mask does not prevent parallelism, it is the rule that makes parallel training possible.

sorular.soru: During translation, when the decoder predicts the token 'ours', where do Q, K and V in cross-attention come from?
secenekler: Q, K and V all come from the decoder's current target-prefix state
Q comes from the encoder memory H_enc; K and V come from the decoder prefix state
Q comes from the decoder state h_t; K and V come from the encoder output H_enc
Q and K come from the decoder; V comes from the raw token embeddings of the source sentence
sorular.aciklama: Q = h_t W_Q (decoder), K = H_enc W_K and V = H_enc W_V (encoder); the decoder asks 'what should I fetch', the source states match it and supply the content. All three coming from the same sequence is the definition of self-attention, not of cross-attention.

sorular.soru: When running inference with an encoder–decoder Transformer, which statement is correct at each new target-token generation step?
secenekler: H_enc is computed once and reused at every step; the decoder takes the growing target prefix
The source sentence is fed to the decoder again at every step and the encoder stack is rerun from scratch
The decoder takes only the state of the last source token from the encoder and uses only that
The decoder generates the entire target sentence at once, fully in parallel, without a causal mask
sorular.aciklama: H_enc is reused at every decoder step; the decoder's input is not the source sentence but the target prefix, which grows by one token at each step (<BOS> → <BOS> Un → ...). Computing the whole target in parallel at once is the training view (under a causal mask), not the inference view.

sorular.konu: Model families: BERT, GPT, T5 and MLM
sorular.soru: What is the rationale for training BERT with Masked Language Modeling (MLM) rather than ordinary next-token prediction?
secenekler: MLM allows the encoder to change the sequence length from layer to layer, unlike decoders
Next-token prediction is defined only in encoder–decoder models that contain cross-attention
MLM makes the causal mask unnecessary, so training parallelizes faster than in decoders
A bidirectional encoder sees the right context, so next-token prediction would be trivial
sorular.aciklama: The encoder uses full self-attention, so both left and right context are visible; asking it to predict the next token would lead to 'cheating', so the target information is hidden from the input with [MASK]. The claim that 'it parallelizes faster because the causal mask is unnecessary' is misleading: decoder-only training is also parallel under a causal mask.

sorular.konu: Model families: BERT, GPT, T5 and MLM
sorular.soru: A team will choose a single pretrained model for NER, extractive QA and text embedding generation. which family is best suited to this use?
secenekler: Encoder-only (BERT-style): bidirectional self-attention, masked-token prediction
Decoder-only (GPT-style): causal self-attention, left-to-right next-token prediction
Encoder–decoder (T5-style): encoder + decoder with cross-attention, text-to-text
Decoder-only with the causal mask removed: bidirectional next-token prediction
sorular.aciklama: Encoder-only BERT-style models read the whole input bidirectionally, produce a contextual representation for each token, and are used for classification, retrieval, NER, extractive QA and embeddings. The decoder-only family is for open-ended generation; next-token prediction with the causal mask removed 'cheats' and is not a valid training setup.

sorular.soru: If the context length of a model using standard self-attention is increased from 2,048 to 8,192 tokens, by roughly what factor does the number of attention scores of a single head grow, according to the scaling rule of attention?
sorular.aciklama: The number of scores scales with n²; when n grows 4× (2,048 → 8,192), the number of scores grows 4² = 16× (8192² / 2048² = 16). The answer '4×' is the mistake of assuming cost is linear in sequence length; the relationship is quadratic: 2n tokens give about 4× the scores.
